transcript.text: My Panasonic NN-ST45KWBPQ is sparking inside when I heat soup, little blue flashes on the right-hand wall and a crackling noise. I stopped it. Is it safe?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Stop using the microwave now: switch it off at the socket and unplug it, and don't run it again (not even empty) until we know why it sparked. Never take the outer casing off — parts inside can hold a lethal charge even when it is unplugged. No — do not use it again until it has been checked by a qualified microwave engineer. Blue flashes and crackling are electrical arcing, not normal operation; on the right-hand wall the usual cause is a dirty or burnt waveguide cover, though foil/metal, a metallic-trimmed container, or damaged cavity coating can do it too. With the microwave unplugged, remove the turntable if helpful and inspect the right-hand wall only: look for food splatter, foil or metal, and any burn mark, crack or hole in the small flat cover panel. Do not remove covers or attempt an internal repair. If you find any scorching, damage or a hole, leave it unplugged and arrange repair.

I've unplugged it and had a look. There's no foil or metal in there, just a plastic bowl of soup was in it. On the right wall there's a cardboard-like panel with a black burnt spot and greasy splatter on it, and the rest of the cavity has a lot of old splatter as I've never really cleaned it. There was also a slight burnt smell, and a wisp of smoke from that spot once before it stopped when I turned it off.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. The burnt cardboard-like panel is the waveguide cover, and it is the most likely source of the arcing. Grease and food deposits can carbonise, then spark and burn through the cover; the smoke and burnt smell mean it must stay unplugged and not be used again. A qualified microwave engineer needs to inspect the cavity behind and around that cover for damaged paint or exposed metal, then determine whether the waveguide cover alone can be replaced or whether there is cavity damage as well. Do not clean, remove or try to patch the burnt panel yourself, and do not test it with water afterwards.

candidates: Burnt or contaminated waveguide cover on the right-hand cavity wall (high)
Food contamination or a metallic item/foil in the cavity (medium)
Damaged cavity coating or internal high-voltage fault (low)
